# Erasure Coding
MinIO AIStor groups the drives in each server pool into one or more **erasure sets** of the same size. By default, each erasure set can contain 2 to 16 drives. On AIStor Server `RELEASE.2026-02-02T23-40-11Z` or later, you can configure erasure sets of up to 32 drives with the [`MINIO_ERASURE_SET_DRIVE_COUNT`](https://docs.min.io/aistor/reference/aistor-server/settings/core/#env-minio-erasure-set-drive-count) environment variable.

An erasure set spans every node in the poolMinIO AIStor groups drives from every node into one erasure set. Eight nodes each contribute two drives, for a set of sixteen.ERASURE SET16 drives · 8 nodes · 1 erasure setNODE 1NODE 2NODE 3NODE 4NODE 5NODE 6NODE 7NODE 8ONE ERASURE SET · 16 DRIVES · 8 NODES

The above example deployment consists of 8 nodes with 2 drives each. MinIO AIStor initializes with a single erasure set consisting of all 16 drives across all eight nodes.

Erasure set stripe size sets the maximum possible parity of the deployment.

Parity is configurable up to half the erasure setA sixteen drive erasure set supports parity from EC:0 to EC:8.

The above example deployment has an erasure set of 16 drives. This can support parity between `EC:0` and 1/2 the erasure set drives, or `EC:8`.

**You can set the parity value between 0 and 1/2 the erasure set size.**

Shard distribution across an erasure setAn object is split into twelve data shards and four parity shards, one shard per drive across the erasure set.ERASURE SETN = 16 drives · K = 12 data · M = 4 parity · EC:4Parity shardPData shardDNODE 1DDNODE 2DDNODE 3DDNODE 4DDNODE 5DDNODE 6DDNODE 7PPNODE 8PP

The example deployment above has an erasure set size of 16 and a parity of `EC:4`

The erasure set must therefore have at least `K` healthy drives to support read operations.

Read quorum for EC:4 is twelve, so reads still succeed.ERASURE SETN = 16 drives · EC:4 · 2 nodes offline · read quorum K = 12Parity shardPData shardDNODE 1DDNODE 2DDNODE 3DDNODE 4DDNODE 5DDNODE 6DDNODE 7PPNODE 8PPSHARD AVAILABILITY12 of 16 shards readableREAD QUORUM K=12 · METAny twelve shards, data or parity, are enough to reconstruct the object.

This deployment has two offline nodes, resulting in only 12 remaining healthy drives. The object was written with `EC:4` with a read quorum of `K=12`.

**MinIO AIStor requires a minimum of `K` erasure set drives to write an object.**

The erasure set must therefore have at least `K` drives online to support write operations.

Write quorumTwo nodes are offline, leaving twelve drives online. Write quorum for EC:4 is twelve, so writes still succeed.ERASURE SETN = 16 drives · EC:4 · 2 nodes offline · write quorum K = 12Parity shardPData shardDNODE 1DDNODE 2DDNODE 3DDNODE 4DDNODE 5DDNODE 6DDNODE 7PPNODE 8PPSHARD AVAILABILITY12 of 16 shards readableWRITE QUORUM K=12 · METAIStor writes all 16 shards and needs K of them acknowledged.

This deployment has two offline nodes, resulting in only 12 remaining healthy drives. This erasure set maintains write quorum and MinIO AIStor can use it for write operations.

`K` is a _success threshold_, not the number of drives MinIO AIStor writes to. For each PUT, MinIO AIStor:

For example, a 16-drive erasure set with `EC:4` parity always attempts 16 individual drive writes per PUT and tolerates up to 4 unsuccessful writes per object before MinIO AIStor returns an error to the client. A 12-drive erasure set with `EC:3` parity attempts 12 drive writes and requires at least 9 to succeed.

**If parity `EC:M` is exactly 1/2 the erasure set size, write quorum is `K+1`.**

Losing write quorum but keeping read quorumFour of eight nodes are offline under EC:8, isolating exactly half the drives. Eight shards remain, which meets the read quorum of eight but not the write quorum of nine, so the set serves reads and refuses writes.ERASURE SETN = 16 drives · EC:8 · 4 of 8 nodes offline · half the set isolatedParity shardPData shardDNODE 1DDNODE 2DDNODE 3DDNODE 4DDNODE 5PPNODE 6PPNODE 7PPNODE 8PPSHARD AVAILABILITY8 of 16 shards readableREAD QUORUM K=8 · METWRITE QUORUM K+1=9 · LOSTWhen parity is exactly half the set, write quorum is K+1 — this is what stops a split brain writing the same object to both halves.

This deployment has four of its eight nodes offline due to a transient network failure, isolating exactly half the drives in the erasure set. However, the erasure set maintains read quorum (`K=8`) and continues to serve read requests.

When an erasure set loses write quorum but maintains read quorum, MinIO AIStor continues to serve read operations while rejecting write operations until sufficient drives come back online to restore write quorum.

For example, on a 16-drive erasure set with `EC:4` parity where 2 drives are offline, MinIO AIStor writes the object as `EC:6`.

You can change this behavior with the [`MINIO_ERASURE_PARITY_FAILURE`](https://docs.min.io/aistor/reference/aistor-server/settings/storage-class/#env-minio-erasure-parity-failure) setting.

Healing rebuilds the shards that were lostNodes 5 and 6 are offline, so four data shards are unreadable. Healing rebuilds them from the four parity shards on nodes 7 and 8. ERASURE SETN = 16 drives · EC:4 · 2 nodes offline · 4 data shards lostParity shardPData shardDNODE 1DDNODE 2DDNODE 3DDNODE 4DDNODE 5DDNODE 6DDNODE 7PPNODE 8PPREBUILD FROM PARITY

Since the object has maintained **read quorum**, MinIO AIStor can heal those lost data shards using the available parity shards.

Where possible, use an even number of nodes and an even number of drives per node.

# MinIO Erasure Code Quickstart Guide [![Slack](https://camo.githubusercontent.com/14e741f30d35dc19702d6003debd23eaefcf733f746415b27c0d9dd4a30af929/68747470733a2f2f736c61636b2e6d696e2e696f2f736c61636b3f747970653d737667)](https://slack.min.io/)
With the highest level of redundancy, you may lose up to half (N/2) of the total drives and still be able to recover the data.

## What is Erasure Code?
In 12 drive example above, with MinIO server running in the default configuration, you can lose any of the six drives and still reconstruct the data reliably from the remaining drives.

## Why is Erasure Code useful?
For example, RAID6 can protect against two drive failure whereas in MinIO erasure code you can lose as many as half of drives and still the data remains safe. Further, MinIO's erasure code is at the object level and can heal one object at a time. For RAID, healing can be done only at the volume level which translates into high downtime. As MinIO encodes each object individually, it can heal objects incrementally.

## How are drives used for Erasure Code?
MinIO divides the drives you provide into erasure-coding sets of _2 to 16_ drives. Therefore, the number of drives you present must be a multiple of one of these numbers.

Minio uses the largest possible EC set size which divides into the number of drives given. For example, _18 drives_ are configured as _2 sets of 9 drives_, and _24 drives_ are configured as _2 sets of 12 drives_.

The drives should all be of approximately the same size.

## Get Started with MinIO in Erasure Code
### 2. Run MinIO Server with Erasure Code
```
podman run \
  -p 9000:9000 \
  -p 9001:9001 \
  --name minio \
  -v /mnt/data1:/data1 \
  -v /mnt/data2:/data2 \
  -v /mnt/data3:/data3 \
  -v /mnt/data4:/data4 \
  -v /mnt/data5:/data5 \
  -v /mnt/data6:/data6 \
  -v /mnt/data7:/data7 \
  -v /mnt/data8:/data8 \
  quay.io/minio/minio server /data{1...8} --console-address ":9001"
```

# Core Operational Concepts [Permalink to this heading](https://minio.community/community/minio-object-store/operations/concepts.html#core-operational-concepts)
## [How does MinIO provide availability, redundancy, and reliability?](https://minio.community/community/minio-object-store/operations/concepts.html#id10) [Permalink to this heading](https://minio.community/community/minio-object-store/operations/concepts.html#how-does-minio-provide-availability-redundancy-and-reliability)
### [MinIO Uses](https://minio.community/community/minio-object-store/operations/concepts.html#id11) [Erasure Coding](https://minio.community/community/minio-object-store/operations/concepts/erasure-coding.html#minio-erasure-coding) for Data Redundancy and Reliability [Permalink to this heading](https://minio.community/community/minio-object-store/operations/concepts.html#minio-uses-erasure-coding-for-data-redundancy-and-reliability)
Erasure Coding provides object-level [healing](https://minio.community/community/minio-object-store/operations/concepts/healing.html#minio-concepts-healing) with significantly less overhead than adjacent technologies such as RAID or replication.

### [MinIO Implements Bit Rot Healing to Protect Data At Rest](https://minio.community/community/minio-object-store/operations/concepts.html#id12) [Permalink to this heading](https://minio.community/community/minio-object-store/operations/concepts.html#minio-implements-bit-rot-healing-to-protect-data-at-rest)
If an object becomes corrupted by bit rot, MinIO can automatically [heal](https://minio.community/community/minio-object-store/operations/concepts/healing.html#minio-concepts-healing) the object depending on the availability of parity shards for the object.

### [MinIO Automatically Heals Corrupt or Missing Data On-the-fly](https://minio.community/community/minio-object-store/operations/concepts.html#id14) [Permalink to this heading](https://minio.community/community/minio-object-store/operations/concepts.html#minio-automatically-heals-corrupt-or-missing-data-on-the-fly)
[Healing](https://minio.community/community/minio-object-store/operations/concepts/healing.html#minio-concepts-healing) is MinIO’s ability to restore data after some event causes data loss.

# Erasure Coding 101
May 29, 2025

## Overview of MinIO Erasure Coding
Even if you lose as many as 7 ((n/2)–1) drives, be it parity or data, you can still reconstruct the data reliably from the remaining drives.

An erasure set is basically a set of drives, and a cluster consists of one or more erasure sets, determined by the amount of total disks.

We can configure our four nodes with 100 drives each to use an erasure set size of 16, the default. Every 16 drives is one erasure set made up of 8 data and 8 parity drives. In this case, the erasure set is based on 400 physical drives, divided equally into data and parity drives, and can tolerate the loss of up to 175 drives.

When a large object, ie. greater than 10 MB, is written to MinIO, the S3 API breaks it into a multipart upload. S3 requires each part to be at least 5 MB (except the last part) and no more than 5 GB. Imagine an object that is 320 MB.

The default erasure set in MinIO is 12 data and 4 parity, meaning that as long as MinIO can read any 12 drives the object can be served.

## Benefits of Erasure Coding and MinIO’s Implementation
Not only does MinIO erasure coding protect objects against data loss in the event that multiple drives and nodes fail, MinIO also protects and heals at the object level. The ability to heal one object at a time is a dramatic advantage over RAID that heals at the volume level. If a drive goes bad and is replaced, MinIO recognizes the new drive, adds it to the erasure set, and then verifies objects across all drives.
